keyVerseText: I have sinned; what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men? why hast thou set me as a mark against thee, so that I am a burden to myself?
rootMeaning: The root of מִפְגָּע (miphgâʻ) is פָּגַע (pâgaʻ), which conveys the idea of encountering or meeting, often with an element of impact or coming between. This root suggests not merely a passive meeting but an active reaching or falling upon, sometimes with force or intent. Thus, מִפְגָּע carries the sense of something that has been struck or targeted, emphasizing the reality of being met or affected directly rather than a neutral encounter.
usageInScripture: This noun appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Job 7:20, where it is translated as 'me as a mark.' This singular usage highlights its meaning as an object of attack or a target, a focus of assault or suffering. The consistency in translation underscores the word’s function to denote a person or thing that has been singled out or struck, revealing a vivid picture of vulnerability and being set apart as a target.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מִפְגָּע as a mark or object of assault deepens our grasp of human suffering and divine interaction in Scripture. It reminds believers that trials and hardships are not random but often felt as being set apart or targeted in a personal way. This word points to the reality of spiritual and physical affliction that can come upon the faithful, yet it also opens the door to recognizing God’s sovereign purpose in allowing such encounters. Theologically, it invites trust in the Preserver of men, who sees beyond the immediate assault to a greater redemptive plan, ultimately fulfilled in Christ’s own suffering and intercession.
keyVerseReflection: In Job 7:20, the speaker laments, 'why hast thou set me as a mark against thee,' expressing a profound sense of being singled out for suffering. The word מִפְגָּע here intensifies the feeling of being a direct target of divine displeasure or trial, making Job’s anguish deeply personal. This highlights the experience of feeling burdened by God’s hand, yet it also opens a space for faith to wrestle with God’s purposes amid pain.
